domain: Navigation model, app structure and native UI patterns/conventions

items.title: Back closes the topmost overlay first: CloseWatcher, <dialog> and popover close requests
items.what: A 'close request' is Esc on desktop or the Android back gesture/button. Modal <dialog>, popover=auto and CloseWatcher instances form one stack, and a close request closes the top item before history goes back. CloseWatcher brings the same behaviour to custom overlays: drawers, sheets, full-screen panels and lightboxes.
items.why: On Android, the biggest web tell is pressing Back with a menu or sheet open and leaving the screen (or the app) instead of just closing the menu. With close requests, Back closes the overlay first, then navigates, the same as a native app.
items.support: CloseWatcher: Chrome/Edge 126+ (desktop and Android), Firefox 149+ (BCD lists Android 149 too, but Firefox's Android back-button wiring is tracked in bug 1966467, so verify), Safari: Technology Preview only (not in Safari 27 or iOS 27). Android Back closing modal <dialog>/popover: Chrome 120+. <dialog>: Baseline 2022 (Safari 15.4). Popover: Baseline Jan 2025 (Chrome 114, Firefox 125, Safari 17).
items.gotchas: Anti-abuse rules: the cancel event fires only when the page has transient user activation, and once per activation. Watchers created without activation are grouped, so one Back closes all of them. Two close requests in a row without activation always go through. You cannot build a 'trap' ("are you sure?" on every Back). Create watchers inside the click/tap handler that opens the overlay. Always destroy() the watcher when the overlay closes some other way, or the next Back is swallowed doing nothing. Don't also listen for keydown Escape for the same overlay: it double-fires on desktop. iOS has no back button. iOS Safari/standalone needs the history fallback (next item) plus a visible close/back affordance. Firefox and Safari types may be missing from older lib.dom.

items.title: History-entry fallback for overlays: one entry per open overlay, never push after a back
items.what: Where CloseWatcher is missing (Safari/iOS, older Firefox), give each open overlay its own same-document history entry (pushState with no URL change). Then browser Back, the iOS edge swipe and history.back() all pop the overlay through popstate.
items.why: It makes the iOS standalone edge-swipe and the browser Back button close sheets and panels instead of leaving the screen. It also keeps a single close path: closing from the UI calls history.back().
items.support: History API: universal. Needed on Safari/iOS (all versions as of Safari 27), Firefox < 149, and any browser without CloseWatcher.
items.gotchas: Chrome's history-manipulation intervention skips entries added without user activation when the user presses the browser/OS Back button (history.back() is unaffected). Push only from a tap/click handler. Field lesson from Threa (PR #2189): a pushState right after a browser-initiated back, with no activation in between, made Chrome mark all the same-document entries skippable, and the next Android Back exited the app. Never re-push a 'sentinel' entry after a back. Keep one entry per overlay, and when an overlay closes while the app has pushed above it, mark its entry stale instead of re-pushing. Forward after a back lands on an overlay entry whose overlay is gone: treat depth > open.length as a no-op or replaceState it down. Playwright does not reproduce the Android skip, so test on a real device. pushState doesn't fire popstate or hashchange.

items.title: Classify every UI state: new screen = pushState, refinement = replaceState, transient = no history
items.what: Use pushState (or a URL push) for a new place the user should be able to go Back from: open a conversation, item detail, settings page. Use replaceState for in-place refinements: filter/sort/tab within a screen, search text, the selected row in a wide master-detail layout, normalising or cleaning a URL. Transient UI (menu, confirm, toast, action sheet) gets no URL and uses close requests.
items.why: Native back stacks contain screens, not every tap. Back that walks through filter toggles or search keystrokes, or an address bar that leaks state, are classic web tells.
items.support: Universal (History API). The (width >= 840px) range syntax needs Chrome 104, Firefox 102 (63 for the feature-first form), Safari 16.4.
items.gotchas: pushState/replaceState never fire popstate or hashchange, so call your router yourself. Search-as-you-type: replace on every keystroke and push once only if the committed search should be a Back step. Keep history.state small (ids, not data); browsers cap its size. replaceState can't remove an entry that's already in history. Strip secrets on the very first load, before any analytics or error reporter reads location.
sources: Yurt: apps/web/src/store.ts (onRoute, invite key stripping, go())

items.title: Navigation API as the router core (with History API fallback)
items.what: window.navigation centralises every same-origin navigation (links, forms, back/forward, history.* calls) into one 'navigate' event that you can intercept, with entries(), currentEntry, keys, per-entry state, traverseTo(key), canGoBack and built-in scroll/focus handling.
items.why: One code path handles link clicks, browser Back, and the iOS/Android back gestures. It also gives precise control of scroll restoration (after content renders) and focus reset, and lets you jump back to a tab's root entry (traverseTo) the way a native tab bar pops to root.
items.support: Navigation API: Chrome/Edge 102 (intercept 105), Firefox 147, Safari 26.2 / iOS 26.2. Baseline newly available since 2026-01-13. NavigateEvent.hasUAVisualTransition: Chrome 118, Firefox 147, Safari 26.2. intercept({precommitHandler}): Chromium (141 per BCD, 146 per web-features) and Firefox 147/148, not Safari.
items.gotchas: Keep a History API fallback: plenty of iPhones are still on iOS < 26.2. TypeScript: older lib.dom lacks these types (use @types/dom-navigation or a TS version that ships them). Hash-only navigations are intercepted too (e.hashChange === true). Traversals generally can't be cancelled. The default focusReset moves focus to <body> after the handler, so set 'manual' if you manage focus. navigation.entries() only lists same-origin entries of this document's session. canGoBack is false on a cold launch or deep link (see Up vs Back).

items.title: Hash vs path routing on static hosts
items.what: Hash routes (#/w/CODE/c/channel) work on any static host and subpath (GitHub Pages /repo/) with one index.html, are never sent to the server, and work offline from a precached shell. Path routes need the host (or a service worker) to serve index.html for every deep URL.
items.why: A deep link or home-screen launch that 404s, or a reload that loses the screen, breaks the illusion of an app. The route must survive reload, share and cold start on every host you deploy to.
items.support: Universal. Service worker navigation fallback: all modern browsers (iOS 11.3+).
items.gotchas: GitHub Pages' 404.html is served with HTTP 404: fine for users, bad for crawlers and link previews. Hash routing conflicts with in-page #anchors (route them through your router) and can't be server-rendered or indexed. Notification, share-target and shortcut URLs must include the hash. Secrets in the fragment don't reach servers but DO reach history, sync and screenshots, so strip them (previous item). With a path router, make every in-scope URL resolvable or the installed app shows the host's 404 on launch.

items.title: Deep links restore the full screen state; parsers never throw
items.what: Encode everything needed to rebuild a screen in its URL (workspace, conversation, open thread/panel, selected tab). Parse it leniently: malformed escapes, unknown segments and stray parts are dropped, never thrown.
items.why: Native apps reopen exactly where a notification or link points. A hand-edited, truncated or old link that crashes or lands on a blank screen is a web tell.
items.support: Routing: universal. Manifest shortcuts: Chrome desktop 96, Chrome Android 84, Safari macOS 17.4 (web apps in Dock); not iOS, not Firefox.
items.gotchas: Validate every segment as untrusted input (it is). Round-trip test parse(build(r)) === r with fuzzing (fixed seed). A link to something not yet loaded (e.g. a thread whose events haven't synced) needs a loading state, not a 'not found'. Distinguish 'first route of this page load came from outside' (deep link) from in-app navigation (Yurt keeps an `entry` flag), because Back behaves differently (next item).

items.title: Up vs Back: an in-app back button that never exits a deep-linked app
items.what: Pushed screens get a visible back control. If the user arrived from inside the app, it performs history Back. If they entered on this screen (notification, shared link, cold launch), it goes Up to the logical parent by replacing the entry, so the app doesn't close or bounce to another site.
items.why: Installed iOS apps have no browser Back button, and desktop standalone windows hide it. Without an in-app back the user is stuck. With a naive history.back() on a deep-linked screen, the app exits or jumps to the referring site.
items.support: Universal. With the Navigation API you can also use navigation.canGoBack (Chrome 102, Firefox 147, Safari 26.2), which is false on a cold launch.
items.gotchas: Routers that navigate via `location.hash = x` leave history.state null, so set the marker with replaceState after the hash change or switch to pushState. After Up, Back from the parent exits the app: that matches Android's synthetic back stack. iOS conventions put back top-left, which is hard to reach on big phones, so also support the edge swipe (next item). In RTL, the back control and swipe edge mirror.
sources: Yurt: apps/web/src/store.ts (entry: 'The first route of a page load came from outside')

items.title: iOS edge-swipe back, custom swipe-to-close, and no double animations
items.what: iOS home-screen web apps have had a system edge swipe for history back/forward since iOS 12.2, and Safari tabs have the same gesture. Make full-screen panels history entries so the system swipe closes them. Add your own swipe-right-to-close for panels on narrow screens, and skip your own transition when the browser already animated the navigation (hasUAVisualTransition).
items.why: It reproduces the iOS navigation-stack feel. It also avoids two web tells: a swipe that leaves the app instead of closing the panel, and a page that slides twice (Safari's snapshot slide, then your view transition).
items.support: Edge-swipe back in iOS standalone web apps: iOS 12.2+. PopStateEvent.hasUAVisualTransition: Chrome 118, Firefox 149, Safari 18. NavigateEvent.hasUAVisualTransition: Chrome 118, Firefox 147, Safari 26.2.
items.gotchas: In iOS standalone mode the system edge swipe can't be disabled; overscroll-behavior-x does not stop it (multiple reports). If a full-screen panel is NOT a history entry, the system swipe navigates away from the whole screen. Several frameworks (Astro, Nuxt, TanStack Router) shipped fixes for the double-animation/flicker on Safari swipe-back by checking hasUAVisualTransition. The swipe distance thresholds above are Yurt's field-tested values, not platform constants. The system edge width (~20-30px) isn't documented.

items.title: Preserve state: scroll per screen and resume the last screen on relaunch
items.what: Remember each screen's scroll offset (keyed by route or history entry key) and restore it on Back. Start pushed screens at the top. On a cold launch with no deep link, resume the last route plus drafts and selections.
items.why: Native back stacks keep each screen exactly as it was left, and iOS evicts background web apps often. Losing your place on Back or relaunch is a top web tell.
items.support: history.scrollRestoration: Chrome 46, Firefox 46, Safari 11. pagehide: universal. content-visibility: hidden: Chrome 85, Firefox 125, Safari 18. Navigation API alternative: intercept({ scroll: 'manual' }) + e.scroll().
items.gotchas: App-shell layouts (body overflow hidden plus an inner scroller, like Yurt) get no browser restoration at all. Restore only after the content has its final height: reserve image space with width/height or aspect-ratio. Chat views anchor to the bottom instead: restore 'distance from bottom', not scrollTop. pagehide/visibilitychange-hidden is the last reliable moment on iOS; unload and beforeunload are unreliable and block bfcache. Don't resume into a confirm/payment/expired-auth screen. Only resume when launched without an explicit deep link.

items.title: External links and app scope: leave the app deliberately, never by accident
items.what: Keep navigations inside the manifest scope. Open off-scope and external links with target=_blank rel=noopener so the OS shows its in-app browser or the default browser, and the installed app's own window doesn't navigate off-site.
items.why: An installed app whose window turns into a random website (with a URL bar suddenly appearing, or no way back on iOS) is the most jarring web tell.
items.how: Docs // Catch-all for user content (markdown, chat messages): document.addEventListener('click', (e) => { const a = e.target instanceof Element ? e.target.closest('a[href]') : null; if (!(a instanceof HTMLAnchorElement) || a.target) return; const url = new URL(a.href, location.href); if (url.origin !== location.origin) { a.target = '_blank'; a.rel = 'noopener noreferrer'; } }); // Manifest: scope is what 'inside the app' means // { "start_url": "./", "scope": "./" } // Chromium desktop only: own several origins as one app with "scope_extensions" plus // /.well-known/web-app-origin-association on each extra origin (check the exact member shape in Chrome's docs).
items.support: target=_blank: universal. Out-of-scope navigation in installed apps: Chrome Android shows a custom-tab-like toolbar; Chrome desktop shows an origin bar with 'open in browser'; iOS standalone hands links to an in-app Safari view or Safari, and the behaviour has varied by iOS version. scope_extensions: Chrome/Edge 138 desktop (Win/macOS/Linux/ChromeOS); not mobile, Safari or Firefox.
items.gotchas: iOS home-screen apps have storage (cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB) separate from Safari, so a login done in Safari doesn't exist in the app. Run OAuth/SSO and return to an in-scope URL inside the app, and test it in the installed app on every OS. Since iOS 26, every site added to the Home Screen opens as a web app by default (users can switch 'Open as Web App' off), so these rules apply even without a manifest. Unverified: the exact iOS 26/27 behaviour for window.open versus target=_blank. Test both. mailto:/tel: links hand off to the OS and are fine. Never put credentials or tokens in links you open externally.

items.title: Single-window launches: launch_handler, launchQueue and link capturing
items.what: launch_handler.client_mode controls whether launches (icon, link, share, file, protocol) reuse the existing app window. focus-existing plus launchQueue lets the running app route the target URL itself. Since Chrome 139 on desktop, clicking a link to an installed app's scope opens it in the app by default.
items.why: Native chat or mail apps don't spawn a second copy (with a second connection) every time you click a link or notification. They bring the existing window forward and navigate inside it.
items.support: launch_handler: Chrome/Edge 110. launchQueue is desktop only (BCD: no Chrome Android); the Chromium intent said desktop only. Default navigation capturing into installed PWAs: Chrome 139 on Windows/macOS/Linux, ChromeOS later. handle_links ('preferred'): Chromium, experimental. Firefox and Safari: none of these. clients.openWindow: universal (Safari/iOS 11.1/11.3+). WindowClient.navigate: Safari 16+.
items.gotchas: The array form lists fallbacks in order. Users can switch link capturing off per app in Chrome's app settings. Test the cold-launch path too: launchQueue fires for the initial launch as well. Don't rely on these for correctness on mobile. Make the SW notificationclick path robust instead. ServiceWorker types need the webworker lib in a separate tsconfig.

items.title: Multiple windows and tabs: one leader, shared state, and which window is 'active'
items.what: Desktop users open the app in several tabs or windows (and tabbed-mode apps on ChromeOS). Coordinate them: elect one leader for the expensive live connection with Web Locks, fan out updates with BroadcastChannel, and decide presence, sounds and 'mark as read' from visibility plus focus.
items.why: Duplicate notifications and sounds, unread counts that disagree between windows, or showing 'online' while every window is hidden: native apps never do this.
items.support: BroadcastChannel: Chrome 54, Firefox 38, Safari 15.4. Web Locks: Chrome 69, Firefox 96, Safari 15.4. document.hasFocus/visibilityState: universal. display_override 'tabbed': Chrome 126 per BCD, but shipped for ChromeOS; on other desktops it's not on by default (verify). Window Management API (getScreenDetails): Chromium only, permission-gated.
items.gotchas: Only mark messages read when the window is visible AND focused AND the message is in view. A window behind others on desktop can still report 'visible'. Headless test browsers always report visible: Yurt keeps presenceNow() to one line with a coverage ignore. iOS home-screen apps are single-window, and window.open there opens an in-app browser. In installed desktop Chromium apps, an in-scope window.open opens a new app window, and each window has its own history stack. Idle Detection API is Chromium-only and permission-gated; avoid it for presence.

items.title: Window Controls Overlay: your own title bar on desktop installs
items.what: With display_override window-controls-overlay, an installed desktop app draws into the title-bar area and the OS window buttons float over it. You position content with env(titlebar-area-*) and mark drag regions with app-region.
items.why: Native desktop apps (Slack, VS Code, Teams) put search, tabs and account controls in the title bar. A thin browser-style title bar above your own header wastes about 30px and looks like a browser window.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 105+ on desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS). Not Android, Safari or Firefox (Firefox's Windows taskbar web apps, 143+, keep an address bar). The env(titlebar-area-*) variables need Chrome 93 (Linux from 93). -webkit-app-region: Chromium.
items.gotchas: Only applies when installed, and the user can collapse the overlay back to a normal title bar, so design both states. Drag regions swallow clicks: every interactive child needs no-drag. Keep the title bar's colour in sync with theme-color and dark mode. Leave room for the OS buttons: their side differs on macOS and Windows, so use the env() values, never hard-coded padding. Make sure your sticky header doesn't also sit under the overlay.

items.title: Window and tab title carry context and unread count
items.what: document.title names the current screen and prefixes an unread count. Installed Chromium apps can set the title-bar text separately with <meta name="application-title">.
items.why: Native windows show the document or conversation in the title bar and task switcher. The tab strip, history menu and Alt-Tab are where users see unread state.
items.support: document.title: universal. application-title: Chrome/Edge 134+, Opera 119, Samsung Internet 29; not Firefox or Safari. Non-standard (not in the WHATWG MetaExtensions registry).
items.gotchas: Don't flash or alternate titles to grab attention: it's hostile and screen readers may re-announce. Use the favicon/app badge instead. Update the title on every route change, which is also good for history and bookmarks. The exact composition of the installed-app title bar (app name plus document title) varies by platform; verify.

items.title: Favicon and app-icon badges reflect live state
items.what: Draw the tab icon on a canvas from the declared icon, adding a numbered badge for mentions, a dot for other unread, a ring while in a call, and grey-out when offline. Restore the original when there's nothing to say. Mirror the count to the OS app icon with the Badging API when installed.
items.why: Native apps badge their dock or taskbar icon. Pinned tabs and installed apps are where users glance for 'anything new?'.
items.support: Dynamic favicon: Chromium and Firefox tabs. Safari shows favicons, but how reliably it picks up runtime data: URL changes is unverified. setAppBadge: Chrome/Edge desktop 81 (Windows/macOS), ChromeOS 91, not Chrome Android (Android badges come from notifications); Safari 17 for macOS web apps; iOS/iPadOS 16.4+ for Home Screen web apps. In Safari, setAppBadge(0) clears.
items.gotchas: At 16px only about 2 characters fit, so cap at '9+'. Re-render on visibilitychange and when the theme changes. On iOS the badge only shows for Home Screen apps, and in practice needs notification permission. Clear the badge when the user reads things on any window or device, not just this one. Keep the canvas logic in one module with stop() for tests (Yurt's tests stop theirs so they don't fight over the next page's icon).

items.title: Adaptive navigation: bottom tab bar on phones, rail or sidebar on wider windows
items.what: Pick the navigation chrome by window width, not by device: a bottom navigation/tab bar in compact windows (<600px), a navigation rail at medium widths (600-839px), and a persistent sidebar or drawer when expanded (>=840px). Detail panels go full screen when narrow.
items.why: A desktop sidebar squeezed onto a phone, or a hamburger menu as the only navigation, reads as a 'responsive website'. Bottom tabs on phones and sidebars on desktop match each platform's own apps.
items.support: Media range syntax: Chrome 104, Firefox 102, Safari 16.4. dvh: Chrome 108, Firefox 101, Safari 15.4. env(safe-area-inset-*): Chrome 69, Firefox 65, Safari 11 (needs viewport-fit=cover). Container queries (for components): Chrome 105, Firefox 110, Safari 16.
items.gotchas: iPad Split View/Slide Over, foldables and narrow desktop windows all cross breakpoints at runtime, so relayout must keep route, scroll and drafts. Collapsing master-detail: the detail becomes a pushed screen (and Back closes it). Expanding shows both panes. Never hide primary destinations behind a hamburger on phones when there are 3-5 of them. Breakpoints follow Material 3 window size classes; Apple uses size classes (compact/regular) with similar intent.
sources: Yurt: apps/web/src/ui/Panels.tsx (narrow: fixed inset 0 full-screen panel)

items.title: Tab bar conventions and the thumb zone
items.what: Use 3-5 top-level destinations with icon plus short label. Re-tapping the active tab scrolls to top, and a second tap pops to the tab's root. Each tab keeps its own stack and scroll. Put primary actions in the bottom third, and keep destructive actions away from easy accidental reach.
items.why: These are muscle-memory behaviours from iOS and Android. Missing them, or putting the main action top-right on a 6.7" phone, feels foreign.
items.support: Pattern, no API. scrollTo smooth: universal (Safari 15.4+ for smooth).
items.gotchas: Respect prefers-reduced-motion for the scroll-to-top. Hide the tab bar while the keyboard is up on Android, or it rides on top of the keyboard (interactive-widget=resizes-content). A FAB or composer goes above the tab bar, not under the home indicator. On iPadOS the tab bar lives at the top or becomes a sidebar. Unverified: iOS 'tap the status bar to scroll to top' only reaches the document scroller, not inner overflow containers. If you rely on it, scroll the document.

items.title: Large titles and sticky translucent headers (and Safari 26 toolbar tinting)
items.what: A sticky header with a translucent, blurred material, plus a large title that collapses into the bar as content scrolls. Use scroll-driven animations where supported and an IntersectionObserver class toggle elsewhere.
items.why: iOS large titles and blurred bars, and Material's top app bar that lifts on scroll, are signature native details. Since Safari 26 the header also decides the colour of Safari's own toolbars.
items.support: backdrop-filter: Chrome 76, Firefox 103, Safari 18 unprefixed (-webkit- since Safari 9). Scroll-driven animations: Chrome 115, Safari 26; Firefox only in preview/flag. prefers-reduced-transparency: Chrome 118 only (Firefox behind flag, no Safari).
items.gotchas: Put `animation-timeline` AFTER the `animation` shorthand, which resets it. Safari 26+ (iOS/macOS browser tabs) ignores theme-color and tints its Liquid Glass toolbars from a position:fixed/sticky element touching the top/bottom edge and spanning most of the width, using that element's own background-color (and backdrop-filter). It does not sample pseudo-elements or absolutely positioned children. A mostly transparent header gives odd tints, so give the header element itself an opaque-enough background. Blur is GPU-expensive on low-end Android, and an opaque fallback is fine. Set z-index above content but below dialogs and popovers (top layer handles those).

items.title: System font stack and platform type conventions
items.what: Use the OS UI font (SF Pro on Apple, Segoe UI on Windows, Roboto/Google Sans on Android) through system-ui, plus the OS monospace font. Use tabular numerals for counts and times.
items.why: Text is most of an app's surface. A web font for UI text is an instant 'website' signal, and the system font also matches menus, pickers and the OS chrome around the app.
items.support: system-ui: Chrome 56, Firefox 92, Safari 11 (-apple-system since Safari 9). ui-monospace/ui-rounded/ui-serif: Safari only (others fall through the stack). text-wrap: balance: Chrome 114, Firefox 121, Safari 17.5.
items.gotchas: A brand font for headings or marketing is fine. Keep body and controls on system-ui. Unverified, often reported: system-ui on Windows in some CJK locales resolves to a font that renders Latin poorly. If that matters, list 'Segoe UI' first on Windows. Don't set -webkit-font-smoothing globally for light-on-dark only; test both themes.

items.title: Respect the user's text size: rem everywhere, iOS Dynamic Type, Chromium text-scale
items.what: Size all text in rem/em from the user's default size. On iOS, opt into Dynamic Type with font: -apple-system-body so the Settings › Text Size slider applies. In Chromium, opt into the OS text scale with <meta name="text-scale" content="scale">.
items.why: Native apps grow with the OS accessibility text size. Most websites don't, which makes them unreadable for many users and is a measurable parity gap.
items.how:
<meta name="text-scale" content="scale"> <!-- Chromium 146+: initial font size follows the OS text scale -->

html { font-size: 100%; -webkit-text-size-adjust: 100%; text-size-adjust: 100%; }
/* iOS only: -webkit-touch-callout exists only in iOS Safari, so macOS Safari (which would shrink to its small
   fixed system size) is excluded */
@supports (font: -apple-system-body) and (-webkit-touch-callout: none) {
  html { font: -apple-system-body; } /* ~17px at the default setting, scales with Dynamic Type */
  body { font-family: var(--font-ui); } /* keep your family; the size stays dynamic */
}
body { font-size: 1rem; } h1 { font-size: 1.75rem; } .caption { font-size: .8125rem; }
/* Fields: keep >= 16px on touch so iOS doesn't zoom on focus, but still scale up with the user */
@media (pointer: coarse) { input, textarea, select { font-size: max(16px, 1rem); } }
/* Finer control in Chromium: calc(1rem * env(preferred-text-scale, 1)) */
items.support: -apple-system-body Dynamic Type: iOS/iPadOS Safari and WKWebView; not macOS. meta text-scale: Chrome/Edge 146 (experimental). env(preferred-text-scale): Chrome 138 (experimental). Per the explainer it is effective on mobile first, with Windows support in progress. Firefox and Safari: neither.
items.gotchas: Any px font-size breaks the chain. So do html { font-size: 62.5% } tricks unless everything else is rem. Layouts must reflow at 200%+: no fixed-height rows, allow wrapping, test with the largest accessibility sizes. Yurt forces 16px!important on fields for coarse pointers to stop iOS focus zoom. That also stops fields from growing with Dynamic Type, which max(16px, 1rem) fixes. Don't use maximum-scale or user-scalable=no to stop zoom: it blocks pinch zoom and fails axe. -webkit-text-size-adjust: 100% (not none) prevents iOS landscape text inflation without disabling zoom.

items.title: color-scheme, light-dark() and accent-color: native controls that match the theme
items.what: Declaring color-scheme makes the UA render scrollbars, form controls, date pickers, autofill and the default canvas in light or dark. light-dark() expresses theme tokens in one declaration. accent-color tints checkboxes, radios, range sliders and progress bars with the brand colour.
items.why: White scrollbars and white native pickers inside a dark app, or default-blue checkboxes in a green app, are instant web tells.
items.how:
<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> <!-- applies before CSS loads: no white flash -->

:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
  accent-color: var(--brand);
  --surface: light-dark(#ffffff, #161614);
  --text: light-dark(#1b1b18, #ededea);
}
:root[data-theme='light'] { color-scheme: light; } /* manual override also flips native controls */
:root[data-theme='dark'] { color-scheme: dark; }
.scroller { scrollbar-width: thin; scrollbar-color: var(--scroll-thumb) transparent; scrollbar-gutter: stable; }
items.support: color-scheme: Chrome 81, Firefox 96, Safari 13 (Baseline). light-dark(): Chrome 123, Firefox 120, Safari 17.5 (Baseline 2024). accent-color: Chrome 93, Firefox 92, Safari 15.4. Automatic contrast adjustment is only complete from Safari 26.2, and still partial on Chrome Android. scrollbar-color: Chrome 121, Firefox 64, Safari 26.2. scrollbar-width: Safari 18.2.
items.gotchas: light-dark() only works for colours, and only when color-scheme allows both. accent-color doesn't style <select> or text inputs. On Chrome Android and older Safari, accent-color may not keep the checkmark legible, so pick an accent with good contrast against white and black. scrollbar-color replaces ::-webkit-scrollbar styling in Chromium when both are set.

items.title: Dark mode: follow the system, allow a manual override, keep theme-color in sync, no flash
items.what: The default theme follows prefers-color-scheme, or a deliberate brand default (Yurt defaults to dark). The user can override it to light or dark, stored per device. The override is applied by an inline script before first paint, and every theme change updates <meta name="theme-color"> so the status bar or title bar matches.
items.why: A light status bar over a dark app, or a white flash on launch, gives away the browser underneath. Following the OS automatically is what native apps do.
items.how:
<!-- <head>, before stylesheets -->
<meta name="theme-color" content="#161614">
<script>
  try { const t = localStorage.getItem('theme'); if (t === 'light' || t === 'dark') document.documentElement.dataset.theme = t; } catch {}
</script>

// app
type Theme = 'system' | 'light' | 'dark';
const prefersDark = matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)');
export function applyTheme(t: Theme): void {
  const root = document.documentElement;
  if (t === 'system') delete root.dataset.theme; else root.dataset.theme = t;
  try { localStorage.setItem('theme', t); } catch { /* private mode */ }
  // One theme-color, always the real page surface: media-attribute pairs can't express a manual override.
  const meta = document.querySelector<HTMLMetaElement>('meta[name="theme-color"]');
  if (meta) meta.content = getComputedStyle(document.body).backgroundColor;
}
prefersDark.addEventListener('change', () => applyTheme(savedTheme()));
items.support: theme-color: Chrome Android 92+ (browser tab, except when the device is in dark mode, and installed apps). Chrome/Edge desktop: installed apps only (title bar). Safari 15+, but from Safari 26 only for installed web apps; browser tabs tint from page content (previous items). Firefox: no. prefers-color-scheme: Chrome 76, Firefox 67, Safari 12.1/iOS 13.
items.gotchas: Manifest theme_color/background_color are static: they colour the splash screen and the initial title bar before your JS runs, so pick neutral values or your default theme's. There's no widely shipped dark variant in the manifest. Yurt ships a static theme-color #161614 equal to its dark --surface-page. A manual switch to light leaves the installed app's title or status bar dark unless you sync it as above. iOS standalone status bar: apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style=black-translucent draws content under a white-text status bar (pad with env(safe-area-inset-top)). Whether runtime changes to it apply without relaunch is unverified; assume they don't. Also update canvas-drawn assets (favicon badge colours) on theme change.
sources: https://github.com/mdn/browser-compat-data (html.elements.meta.name.theme-color, notes: 'From Safari 26, the theme color is only used for installed web apps')

items.title: Modals with <dialog>: showModal, requestClose, closedby and invoker commands
items.what: <dialog>.showModal() gives the top layer, a ::backdrop, inertness of the rest of the page, focus containment, Esc and Android-Back handling, and focus return. requestClose() routes app-initiated closes through 'cancel' (for unsaved-changes checks). closedby='any' adds light dismiss. commandfor/command open and close it without JS.
items.why: Hand-rolled div modals leak focus, scroll the page behind, ignore Back and Esc, and stack wrongly. The platform dialog behaves like the OS's own.
items.how:
Delete #general?

 const dlg = document.querySelector('#confirm'); dlg?.addEventListener('close', () => { if (dlg.returnValue === 'delete') remove(); }); dlg?.addEventListener('cancel', (e) => { if (hasUnsavedChanges()) { e.preventDefault(); askDiscard(); } }); // Light-dismiss fallback where closedby isn't supported (Safari as of 27) if (dlg && !('closedBy' in HTMLDialogElement.prototype)) { dlg.addEventListener('click', (e) => { const r = dlg.getBoundingClientRect(); const outside = e.clientX < r.left || e.clientX > r.right || e.clientY < r.top || e.clientY > r.bottom; if (e.target === dlg && outside) 'requestClose' in dlg ? dlg.requestClose() : dlg.close(); }); } /* stop the page behind from scrolling */ html:has(dialog:modal) { overflow: hidden; }
items.support: <dialog>: Baseline 2022 (Chrome 37, Firefox 98, Safari 15.4). requestClose(): Chrome 134, Firefox 139, Safari 18.4 (Baseline May 2025). closedby: Chrome 134, Firefox 141, Safari Technology Preview only. commandfor/command: Chrome 135, Firefox 144, Safari 26.2 (Baseline Dec 2025). Android Back closes a modal dialog: Chrome 120+.
items.gotchas: A preventDefault in cancel is honoured only with user activation (close-watcher anti-abuse), so the second Esc or Back closes anyway. Don't rely on it for data safety: autosave drafts. The rect check is needed because clicks on the dialog's own padding also have target === dialog. Animate entry and exit with @starting-style plus transition-behavior: allow-discrete; the `overlay` property is Chromium-only, so exit animations may cut off elsewhere. Toasts rendered outside the top layer sit under, and are inert beneath, an open modal (see toasts). Non-modal show() doesn't make the rest inert.

items.title: Menus and popovers: Popover API plus CSS anchor positioning
items.what: [popover] puts menus, pickers and callouts in the top layer with light dismiss, Esc and Android Back. CSS anchor positioning tethers them to their button and flips them when they would overflow the viewport, with no JS positioning library.
items.why: Native menus never get clipped by overflow:hidden parents, always close on outside tap or Back, and flip near screen edges. Clipped or mispositioned dropdowns are a classic web tell.
items.how: #more { anchor-name: --more; } #more-menu { position-anchor: --more; position-area: block-end span-inline-start; margin: 4px 0; position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline; } @supports not (anchor-name: --a) { /* fallback: position in JS on 'toggle' (e.g. Floating UI), or centre as a sheet on phones */ } // Right-click/long-press menus at a point: move an invisible fixed 'anchor' element to the pointer, then showPopover().
items.support: Popover: Chrome 114, Firefox 125, Safari 17 (Baseline Jan 2025). Anchor positioning: Chrome 125 (position-try-fallbacks 128, position-area 129; older names inset-area/position-try-options), Firefox 147, Safari 26. web-features does not yet mark it Baseline because some sub-features are incomplete. showPopover({source}) complete in Chrome 137, Firefox 144, Safari 26.
items.gotchas: role=menu commits you to roving-focus arrow-key handling. For a simple action list, plain buttons in a popover are more honest. Nested popovers form a stack only when the child is inside, or invoked from, the parent. On phones, prefer an action sheet (next item) over a tiny anchored menu. Popovers in the top layer escape transforms and overflow, but your z-index scale doesn't apply to them. Older Chrome builds (125-128) used different property names, so test the fallback branch.

items.title: Action sheets and bottom sheets on touch, anchored menus on desktop
items.what: On coarse-pointer or compact screens, present choices as a bottom sheet: a <dialog> pinned to the bottom edge, with safe-area padding, a drag handle, destructive actions in red, and a separate Cancel. On desktop, the same actions appear as an anchored menu.
items.why: Thumb-reachable bottom sheets are how iOS and Android present contextual actions. Centred desktop-style modals or tiny dropdowns on a phone feel ported.
items.support: <dialog>: Baseline 2022. dvh: Chrome 108, Firefox 101, Safari 15.4. Light dismiss via closedby or the fallback from the dialog item.
items.gotchas: Drag-to-dismiss: put touch-action: none only on the handle or header so the sheet's content still scrolls. Velocity-based dismiss at about 0.5px/ms or past 1/3 of the height. When the iOS keyboard opens inside a sheet, the page pans: size the sheet to the visual viewport (Yurt's lib/viewport.ts --app-height pattern). Cancel must be reachable by Back (dialog does this) and by tapping the backdrop. Keep sheets short; long content should be a pushed screen.

items.title: Native pickers: date/time inputs, showPicker(), native <select>, customizable select
items.what: Use <input type=date|time|datetime-local> and <select> to get the OS pickers: the iOS wheel or calendar, the Android material picker, the desktop calendar. Open them from a tap anywhere on the field with showPicker(). Where a styled dropdown is needed, opt the real <select> into appearance: base-select instead of rebuilding it from divs.
items.why: The OS pickers are exactly what native apps use, with locale, accessibility and haptics included. JS date pickers and div dropdowns on phones are glaring web tells.
items.how: field.addEventListener('click', () => { try { field.showPicker(); } catch { /* no activation or unsupported */ } }); @supports (appearance: base-select) { @media (pointer: fine) { select, ::picker(select) { appearance: base-select; } } /* keep the OS picker on phones unless tested */ }
items.support: showPicker() on input: Chrome 99, Firefox 101, Safari 16. select.showPicker(): Chrome 121, Firefox 122, not Safari (flag in TP). appearance: base-select and ::picker(select): Chrome 135, Safari 27 (iOS/iPadOS 27 too, Sept 2026), Firefox behind a flag (149).
items.gotchas: The value is always ISO (yyyy-mm-dd, HH:mm) while the display follows the browser/OS locale. showPicker() throws without user activation and in cross-origin iframes. WebKit's 'golden rule': icons and swatches in options are additions, never substitutes, so always keep text (visually hidden if needed). Otherwise unsupported browsers and screen readers get empty options. Unverified: whether iOS 27 renders the styled ::picker or keeps the system menu for base-select. Test on device before opting phones in. Don't use datalist as a combobox replacement on iOS (weak UI).

items.title: Switches and segmented controls from real inputs
items.what: Immediate-effect settings use a switch: <input type=checkbox switch role=switch>, native in Safari with an iOS haptic, and a styled checkbox elsewhere. Mutually exclusive views (2-5 options) use a segmented control built from radio inputs.
items.why: Settings screens full of checkboxes, or 'tabs' built from buttons, look like web forms. Real inputs give native semantics, keyboard behaviour (arrow keys in radio groups) and, on iOS, the system switch with its haptic tick.
items.how:
<label class="row">Notifications <input type="checkbox" switch role="switch" name="notify"></label>

// Style the fallback only where the native switch is missing
if (!('switch' in HTMLInputElement.prototype)) document.documentElement.classList.add('no-native-switch');
.no-native-switch input[role=switch] { appearance: none; inline-size: 2.75rem; block-size: 1.625rem; border-radius: 999px; background: var(--track-off); position: relative; transition: background .2s; }
.no-native-switch input[role=switch]::before { content: ''; position: absolute; inset: 2px auto 2px 2px; aspect-ratio: 1; border-radius: 50%; background: #fff; transition: translate .2s; }
.no-native-switch input[role=switch]:checked { background: var(--accent); }
.no-native-switch input[role=switch]:checked::before { translate: 1.125rem 0; }

<fieldset class="segmented"><legend class="sr-only">View</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="view" value="list" checked> List</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="view" value="board"> Board</label>
</fieldset>
.segmented { display: inline-flex; padding: 2px; border: 0; border-radius: 9px; background: var(--fill); }
.segmented input { position: absolute; opacity: 0; }
.segmented label { padding: 6px 12px; border-radius: 7px; }
.segmented label:has(:checked) { background: var(--surface); box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / .2); }
.segmented label:has(:focus-visible) { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); }
items.support: switch attribute: Safari 17.4+ (macOS and iOS); iOS 18 added the haptic on toggle. Chrome and Firefox: not supported (renders a checkbox; role=switch is still announced as a switch). :has(): Chrome 105, Firefox 121, Safari 15.4.
items.gotchas: Switches apply immediately with no Save button. Inside a form that needs submit, use a checkbox. Hacks that toggle hidden switch inputs to fire iOS haptics exist, but they rely on undocumented behaviour that Apple can change. Mirror the switch knob in RTL (translate with the inline direction). Segmented controls swap views in place, so update the URL with replaceState, not push.

items.title: Native disclosure: <details name> accordions, ::details-content, hidden=until-found
items.what: <details>/<summary> gives an accessible disclosure with no JS. The name attribute makes exclusive accordions. ::details-content lets you animate it. hidden="until-found" keeps collapsed content findable by find-in-page and fragment links.
items.why: Settings and FAQ-style groups behave like native collapsible sections, Ctrl+F still finds hidden text, and there's no hand-rolled ARIA to get wrong.
items.how:
<details name="settings" open><summary>Notifications</summary>…</details>
<details name="settings"><summary>Privacy</summary>…</details>

:root { interpolate-size: allow-keywords; } /* Chromium: lets block-size animate to auto */
details::details-content { block-size: 0; overflow: clip; transition: block-size .25s, content-visibility .25s allow-discrete; }
details[open]::details-content { block-size: auto; }
summary { list-style: none; } summary::-webkit-details-marker { display: none; }

<section hidden="until-found" id="advanced">…</section>
advanced.addEventListener('beforematch', () => expandAdvancedUi());
items.support: details name: Chrome 120, Firefox 130, Safari 17.2 (Baseline 2024). ::details-content: Chrome 131, Firefox 143, Safari 18.4. interpolate-size: Chrome 129 only, so other browsers open without the height animation. hidden=until-found: Chrome 102, Firefox 148 (139-147 partial), Safari 26.2 (partial: doesn't scroll to the match). beforematch: Chrome 102, Firefox 139, Safari 26.2.
items.gotchas: Safari doesn't support chaining pseudo-elements after ::details-content. Hide the default marker in Safari with ::-webkit-details-marker. Don't put interactive controls inside <summary>. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.

items.title: inert for off-canvas drawers and backgrounds
items.what: The inert attribute removes a subtree from focus, pointer interaction and the accessibility tree. Use it on a closed off-canvas drawer, and on the main content while a custom (non-<dialog>) overlay is open.
items.why: Tabbing into an invisible, off-screen sidebar, or VoiceOver reading content behind a sheet, are invisible-but-real web tells for keyboard and assistive-tech users.
items.support: inert: Chrome 102, Firefox 112, Safari 15.5 (Baseline 2023).
items.gotchas: For true modals prefer dialog.showModal(), which inerts everything else automatically. Don't inert an ancestor of the element that currently has focus without moving focus first. When the drawer opens, focus its first item. When it closes, return focus to the toggle.

items.title: Toasts and snackbars: top layer, safe areas, live region, bounded queue
items.what: Render toasts in a popover=manual container so they sit in the top layer above modal dialogs. Position them above the tab bar or composer and inside safe areas. Announce through an always-present polite live region, cap the number shown, and dismiss pushed-out toasts properly.
items.why: Snackbars (Android) and banners (iOS) are transient, non-blocking feedback. A toast hidden behind a modal, covering the home indicator, or never announced is a web tell.
items.how: #toasts { inset: auto 0 0 0; margin: 0 auto; border: 0; background: none; display: grid; gap: 8px; pointer-events: none; padding: 0 16px calc(12px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom) + var(--bottom-bar, 0px)); } #toasts > * { pointer-events: auto; } export function showToast(el: HTMLElement, text: string): void { const host = document.getElementById('toasts'); const live = document.getElementById('announcer'); if (!host || !live) return; host.append(el); while (host.children.length > 3) host.firstElementChild?.remove(); // Yurt: at most 3; dismiss pushed-out ones through their own dismiss() so callbacks run if (host.matches(':popover-open')) host.hidePopover(); host.showPopover(); // re-enter the top layer above any dialog opened since live.textContent = text; }
items.support: popover=manual: Chrome 114, Firefox 125, Safari 17. :popover-open: same.
items.gotchas: Top-layer order is insertion order, so re-show after opening a dialog or the toast stays beneath it. A live region that was display:none (a hidden popover) when its text changed often isn't announced, which is why the announcer above is separate and always rendered. Pause auto-dismiss on hover/focus. Toasts with an action (Undo) need more time (Yurt's default is 5s) and keyboard reach. Support swipe-to-dismiss on touch. Never put essential information only in a toast. Keep them clear of the iOS keyboard (visual viewport) and the composer.
sources: Yurt: apps/web/src/store.ts (toast(): at most 3, pushed-out ones dismissed properly)

items.title: Pull-to-refresh, overscroll and accidental history swipes
items.what: Turn off the browser's own pull-to-refresh, bounce and scroll chaining on the app shell with overscroll-behavior. Contain horizontal scrollers so reaching their end doesn't trigger a back/forward swipe. Provide pull-to-refresh only where data is fetched on demand; live data refreshes itself.
items.why: Pulling a chat list and having the whole app reload (losing state) is a browser tell. Native live-data apps (chat, mail with push) update themselves and rarely need a manual refresh.
items.support: overscroll-behavior: Chrome 63, Firefox 59, Safari 16 (partial everywhere until recently: no effect on containers without scrollable overflow; fixed in Chrome 144 and Firefox 150, still partial in Safari).
items.gotchas: Chrome on Android keeps pull-to-refresh in installed (standalone) PWAs, so disable it explicitly. iOS home-screen apps have no pull-to-refresh at all, so a live app needs reconnect-on-visible plus a visible 'Retry' in error states. Never make pull-to-refresh the only way to recover. A custom PTR must not fight the OS: only start it when the scroller is at scrollTop 0 and the gesture is vertical. Unverified: whether overscroll-behavior-x stops Safari macOS trackpad history swipes. It doesn't stop the iOS standalone edge swipe.

items.title: Designed empty, loading, error and offline states on every screen
items.what: Each screen defines four states. Empty explains and offers the primary action. Loading uses a layout-matching skeleton shown only after a short delay. Error says what failed, keeps stale data visible, and offers Retry. Offline shows a banner, queues writes, and marks items pending or failed. Connectivity is judged by real reachability, not navigator.onLine alone.
items.why: Blank white screens, spinners that flash for 50ms, and 'Failed to fetch' strings are web tells. Native apps show cached content, unobtrusive status, and per-item retry.
items.support: navigator.onLine and online/offline events: universal (semantics vary: true on a captive portal or LAN-only connection). aria-busy: widely supported by screen readers.
items.gotchas: Skeletons must match the final layout or you trade a spinner for layout shift. Keep showing cached data under an error banner rather than replacing it. Optimistic UI needs a visible pending, then failed-with-retry, state per item. Distinguish 'loading' from 'not found yet' for deep links to data that's still syncing. Test with DevTools offline AND with a reachable network but a dead backend.
sources: Yurt: apps/web/src/lib/favicon.ts (offline: no network or no relay), apps/web/src/store.ts (online/offline listeners)

items.title: Focus management and accessibility parity on navigation
items.what: On every screen change, move focus to the new screen's heading, update document.title and aria-current, and on Back return focus to the element that opened the screen. Show focus rings only for keyboard (:focus-visible). Don't auto-focus text inputs on touch devices, because it pops the keyboard.
items.why: Native apps move VoiceOver/TalkBack focus to the new screen and back again. SPAs that leave focus on a removed button, or pop the keyboard on every screen change, feel broken to assistive-tech and touch users.
items.support: :focus-visible: Chrome 86, Firefox 85, Safari 15.4. focus({preventScroll}): universal modern. focus({focusVisible}): Chrome 145, Firefox 104, Safari 18.4. Navigation API focusReset: see router item.
items.gotchas: Store the opener's id (not the element) across async renders. Lists re-render, so find it again by id. Don't steal focus on background updates (new messages). Announce them through a polite live region instead. A heading with tabindex=-1 needs no visible ring (:focus-visible usually won't match for programmatic focus after a click). The skip link and landmarks (nav, main, aside with aria-label) are the screen-reader equivalent of a tab bar.
sources: Yurt: apps/web/src/ui/Composer.tsx (autoFocus only with pointer: fine)

items.title: forced-colors and prefers-contrast: survive Windows High Contrast and 'Increase contrast'
items.what: In forced-colors mode (Windows contrast themes), the UA replaces your colours with system colours and removes box-shadows and background images. prefers-contrast reflects 'Increase contrast' (macOS/iOS) and similar settings. Add borders and outlines that keep state visible, and drop translucency.
items.why: Native controls adapt automatically. Web apps whose focus rings, selected tabs or toggles are drawn with box-shadow or background colour alone become invisible.
items.support: forced-colors: Chrome 89, Firefox 89, Safari 16. forced-color-adjust: Chrome 89, Firefox 113, not Safari. prefers-contrast: Chrome 96, Firefox 101, Safari 14.1 / iOS 14.5.
items.gotchas: Yurt's design-system focus ring is box-shadow based (base.css :focus-visible), so it vanishes in forced colors unless you add the transparent outline. Use forced-color-adjust: none only for things like colour swatches or avatars where the colour is the content. Use system colour keywords (Canvas, CanvasText, ButtonText, Highlight, LinkText). Test with Edge or Chrome DevTools' forced-colors emulation.

items.title: RTL: logical properties, dir=auto for user content, mirrored gestures and icons
items.what: Lay out with logical properties (inline/block). Set dir on <html> from the locale, use dir=auto on user-generated text and <bdi> around names. Mirror directional icons, drawer sides, and the swipe-back direction and edge.
items.why: In RTL locales, native apps mirror the whole navigation model: back points right and drawers open from the right. A left-to-right app with Arabic text is an obvious port.
items.how:
{message.text}

{user.name} joined .row { padding-inline: 16px; border-inline-start: 3px solid var(--accent); } .drawer { inset-inline-start: 0; } .icon-back:dir(rtl), .icon-chevron-forward:dir(rtl) { transform: scaleX(-1); } const rtl = getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).direction === 'rtl'; const closeSwipe = rtl ? 'left' : 'right'; // Yurt's swipe-right-to-close becomes swipe-left const drawerTranslate = (x: number) => `translateX(${rtl ? -x : x}px)`; // transforms don't flip automatically
items.support: Logical properties: Baseline (all modern). :dir(): Chrome 120, Firefox 49, Safari 16.4. dir=auto and <bdi>: universal.
items.gotchas: Don't mirror media playback controls, clocks, checkmarks, or logos. Numbers and code stay LTR. Gesture code (dragX, edge zones) must flip, and so must keyframe animations that slide on the x axis. Unverified: whether the iOS standalone system back swipe moves to the right edge in RTL. Test on a device set to an RTL language.

items.title: Keyboard shortcuts and a command palette on desktop
items.what: Use platform-correct modifiers (Cmd on Apple, Ctrl elsewhere), single-key shortcuts only outside text fields, a ⌘K/Ctrl+K command palette, a '?' shortcut sheet, aria-keyshortcuts on controls, and visible key hints only where a keyboard is likely.
items.why: Desktop-class apps (Slack, Linear, VS Code) are driven by the keyboard. Missing shortcuts, or Ctrl shown to Mac users, signal a website.
items.support: KeyboardEvent key/code/isComposing: universal. navigator.userAgentData: Chromium only. Keyboard Lock API: Chromium only and effective only in fullscreen. aria-keyshortcuts: exposed by major screen readers to varying degrees.
items.gotchas: Browser-reserved combos (Cmd/Ctrl+W, T, N, L, Tab, Cmd+Q) can't be reliably overridden in a tab, so don't build on them. Use e.key for characters and e.code for physical positions (layout-independent games/WASD). Shortcuts must not fire during IME composition (CJK input). An iPad with a hardware keyboard can't list web shortcuts in the system ⌘-hold overlay. Yurt shows <Kbd> hints only on wide layouts.

items.title: Context menus: right-click, keyboard and long-press, but not on content
items.what: Give app objects (messages, files, list rows) a custom context menu on right-click, the ContextMenu key or Shift+F10, and long-press on touch. Keep the browser's native menu on text, links, images and inputs inside content.
items.why: Right-click and long-press menus are core desktop and mobile idioms. A browser 'Save image as / Inspect' menu on an app object is a web tell. Killing copy/paste on content is worse.
items.support: contextmenu event: all desktop browsers and Chrome/Firefox Android (fires on touch long-press). Not iOS Safari (BCD: safari_ios no). -webkit-touch-callout: iOS Safari only.
items.gotchas: On Android the contextmenu event and your long-press timer both fire, so dedupe (ignore contextmenu if your long-press already opened, or use contextmenu as the touch long-press on Android). Give haptic feedback when the long-press triggers (vibrate on Android, where supported). An Apple Developer Forums thread reports -webkit-touch-callout: none not working in iOS 26.1 for some elements (unverified scope). Test link and image long-press. Every context-menu action must also be reachable another way (overflow button), since it's not discoverable.

items.title: Text selection off on app chrome, on in content
items.what: Make buttons, tabs, toolbars, headers and nav non-selectable, without the iOS callout and with no image dragging. Explicitly keep selection enabled on message bodies, documents and every input.
items.why: Long-pressing a tab or button and getting a blue text selection or a 'Copy | Look Up' bubble is one of the most recognisable web tells on phones. Accidental drag ghosts of icons on desktop are another.
items.support: user-select unprefixed: Chrome 54, Firefox 69. Safari needs -webkit-user-select (unprefixed only in Technology Preview as of Safari 27). -webkit-touch-callout: iOS only. -webkit-user-drag: Chromium and Safari.
items.gotchas: Never put user-select: none on body or app-wide: it blocks copying content and can break assistive tech. Unverified for current iOS, but cheap insurance: an inherited -webkit-user-select: none has historically made inputs and contenteditable inside it un-editable on iOS, so always re-enable on fields. cursor: default vs pointer is a deliberate choice: be consistent across the app.

items.title: Hover effects and tooltips only on hover-capable pointers
items.what: Gate :hover styles and hover tooltips behind @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine). Tooltips also show on keyboard focus. On touch, use visible labels or long-press instead. Prefer interestfor + popover=hint where available, with a small pointer/focus fallback.
items.why: Sticky hover states after a tap on iOS, and title tooltips that never appear on touch (or appear after a slow delay on desktop), are web tells. Native desktop tooltips appear on hover and focus, and touch platforms don't have them.
items.support: hover/pointer media: universal (Chrome Android 50; some Samsung devices wrongly match hover: hover, per BCD). popover=hint (current spec): Chrome 151, Firefox 153; older partial implementations in Chrome 133-150 and Firefox 149-152; Safari: Technology Preview. interestfor: Chrome 142 only (experimental).
items.gotchas: The feature-detect property name for interest invokers has changed during incubation, so verify it against your target Chrome before relying on it. A tooltip is never the only label: icon-only buttons need an accessible name. Don't use title= for important info: it's invisible on touch and to keyboard users. Tooltip delay about 500ms in, instant when moving between adjacent controls. Dismiss on Esc.

items.title: Adapt to display-mode: installed vs browser tab
items.what: Detect whether the app runs as an installed app (standalone, window-controls-overlay, tabbed) or in a browser tab, and adapt: hide 'Install' prompts, show in-app back and close controls, use safe-area padding, and reserve space for the title bar.
items.why: An installed app that still nags 'Install our app', or has no way back on iOS because it assumed a browser Back button, breaks the illusion immediately.
items.support: display-mode media: Chrome 42, Firefox 47, Safari 13 / iOS 12.2. navigator.standalone: iOS Safari only, non-standard (needs a type guard as shown). iOS/iPadOS 26+: every Home Screen site opens as a web app by default. Firefox 143+ on Windows: taskbar web apps that keep an address bar.
items.gotchas: display: minimal-ui isn't supported by Safari or desktop Firefox (it falls back to browser). The display-mode can change at runtime (a user moves a tab into an app window), so listen for changes. Don't UA-sniff for 'is a phone'. Test the installed app separately on each OS: storage, links and status bar differ from the tab.
